scope: Primary and authoritative source boundaries for the new Introduction and Chapters 1–3. This packet supports production; exact candidate claims must still bind exact source excerpts during self-review.

claims.ruledClaim: AI is best understood as a machine-based system that receives inputs and generates outputs such as content, predictions, recommendations or decisions that may influence physical or virtual environments. A deployed system can combine one or more models with other software and human choices.

sources.title: What is AI? Can you make a clear distinction between AI and non-AI systems?
sources.locator: updated OECD definition and explanatory paragraphs
sources.support: Defines an AI system through inputs, inferred outputs and influence, and explains that systems are typically built by combining one or more models.
sources.scopeLimit: The definition is intentionally technology-neutral; the book's layered diagnostic map is a teaching model, not a claim that every system has identical components.

sources.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)
sources.locator: Executive Summary and AI system definition
sources.support: Treats AI as engineered systems whose outputs can influence environments and whose risks depend on context, design, deployment, use and evaluation.
sources.scopeLimit: A risk-management framework, not a beginner curriculum or product architecture.

claims.freshnessTrigger: Any change to the OECD or NIST definition or to the book's claimed universal system boundary.

claims.ruledClaim: Training and deploying many current AI models occur in data centres containing servers, storage and networking equipment, plus power and cooling infrastructure. AI computation is therefore physical, located and dependent on electricity and working equipment even when the interface feels immaterial.

sources.title: Energy and AI — Energy demand from AI
sources.support: Describes data centres as facilities housing servers, storage, networking and associated equipment and states that AI model training and deployment occur mainly in data centres.
sources.scopeLimit: The evergreen chapter uses the physical relationship, not volatile consumption forecasts. Current quantities belong in dated NewsStand treatment.

claims.freshnessTrigger: Any numerical energy, water, market-share or geographical claim, or a claim about where a particular model runs.

claims.ruledClaim: AI workloads can run on general processors and specialised accelerators such as GPUs or TPUs. Large model work may be distributed across multiple networked devices; the exact hardware and scale depend on the model and task.

sources.title: Machine Learning Glossary — accelerator chip, TPU chip and model parallelism
sources.locator: accelerator chip; TPU chip; model parallelism
sources.support: Defines specialised accelerators and explains that model parallelism distributes model parts across devices.
sources.scopeLimit: Google terminology includes Google-specific hardware examples; no brand is presented as universal.

sources.title: CS336: Language Modeling from Scratch
sources.support: The current course explicitly treats GPUs, TPUs, resource accounting, parallelism, data, training, evaluation and inference as parts of building and operating language models.
sources.scopeLimit: An advanced engineering course used to verify the pipeline, not the reading level or structure of the LAiDIES explanation.

claims.freshnessTrigger: Any named chip generation, performance, price, supplier, facility or scale claim.

claims.ruledClaim: A machine-learning model is the learned structure and parameters that transform input into a prediction or other output. It is a component that can be saved and served, not the complete app, company or decision process.

sources.title: Machine Learning Glossary — model
sources.support: Defines a model as the parameters and structure a system needs to make predictions and notes that models can be saved, restored or copied.
sources.scopeLimit: The broad model definition covers more than generative AI; chapter examples must not collapse every model into an LLM.

claims.freshnessTrigger: Any change to the general model definition or a claim about one named model's architecture or parameters.

claims.ruledClaim: During training, a system uses examples and an objective or loss measure to adjust model parameters. Evaluation and post-training may further test or shape behaviour before deployment. The selected data, objectives and evaluations affect what the resulting model can do and where it fails.

sources.title: training stage — Glossary
sources.support: Defines training as the stage in which a model learns parameters that minimize error against an objective function using training data.
sources.scopeLimit: A concise technical definition; the chapter explains the iterative mechanism without implying one training method for every AI model.

sources.title: CS336: Language Modeling from Scratch
sources.locator: What is this course about? and coursework
sources.support: Separates data collection and cleaning, tokenization, architecture, training, evaluation, inference and post-training in a current language-model pipeline.
sources.scopeLimit: Language-model-specific; other model families can use different representations, objectives and training procedures.

claims.freshnessTrigger: Any claim about a named model's training data, objective, post-training method, evaluation result or release process.

claims.ruledClaim: Inference is the use stage: an already trained model processes new input to produce a prediction or response. Supplying material for one inference is not the same operation as changing the model through training.

sources.title: Machine Learning Glossary — inference
sources.support: Defines inference as applying a trained model to new examples and, for LLMs, generating a response to an input prompt.
sources.scopeLimit: Does not establish whether a provider separately retains or later uses product data for model improvement.

claims.freshnessTrigger: Any provider-specific data-use, retention or model-improvement statement.

claims.ruledClaim: Language models operate on tokens rather than human word counts. Tokens may be whole words, characters or subword pieces depending on the tokenizer. Autoregressive language models generate sequences by repeatedly predicting a next token from the preceding context.

sources.title: Machine Learning Glossary — token, tokenizer, language model and auto-regressive model
sources.locator: token; tokenizer; language model; auto-regressive model
sources.support: Defines token forms, tokenization, language models and next-token autoregressive generation.
sources.scopeLimit: Next-token prediction is a mechanism, not proof of factuality, consciousness, simple lookup or the absence of complex learned capabilities.

claims.freshnessTrigger: Any token count, tokenizer behaviour or named model architecture claim.

claims.ruledClaim: AI includes more than generative language models. Systems may classify, rank, forecast, detect, recommend, generate or control, and products may combine model families and modalities.

sources.title: What is AI? Can you make a clear distinction between AI and non-AI systems?
sources.support: Names machine learning and knowledge-based approaches plus application areas including vision, language, speech and decision support.
sources.scopeLimit: A broad taxonomy; the book uses representative jobs rather than claiming exhaustive model families.

sources.title: Machine Learning Glossary — task and model
sources.support: Provides representative machine-learning tasks and separates generative models from other prediction uses.
sources.scopeLimit: Examples are illustrative, not a product suitability or accuracy verdict.

claims.freshnessTrigger: Any provider catalogue, named model capability or universal claim about multimodality.

claims.ruledClaim: A context window is the bounded token space a model can reference while producing a response. Exact capacity and which materials enter are model- and product-specific; more context does not guarantee that every detail will be used correctly.

sources.title: Machine Learning Glossary — context window and lost-in-the-middle effect
sources.support: Defines a context window in tokens and documents that relevant information can be used unevenly within long contexts.
sources.scopeLimit: Does not specify what one product includes or the capacity of a named model.

sources.title: Context windows — Claude Platform Docs
sources.support: Separates working context from training data and illustrates messages, tool results, images, documents and tool definitions occupying request context.
sources.scopeLimit: Claude API-specific details are examples, not universal product behaviour.

claims.freshnessTrigger: Any named model capacity, context-management behaviour or provider-specific inclusion rule.

claims.ruledClaim: Conversation continuity is managed by surrounding product or API software, which may pass prior turns or link stored response state into a later request. A visible chat history does not by itself prove that every earlier detail was supplied to the model for the current response.

sources.title: Conversation state — OpenAI API
sources.locator: OpenAI APIs for conversation state; previous_response_id
sources.support: Shows both manually managed input history and stateful continuation through a previous response identifier.
sources.scopeLimit: One API design; the general lesson concerns the surrounding system's role.

claims.freshnessTrigger: Any claim that a named product always stores, supplies or exposes a particular prior turn.

claims.ruledClaim: Product memory is a product feature, not a synonym for the model's context window or training. A product may retain selected information separately from chat history and may add it to later response context; controls and behaviour vary.

sources.title: Memory FAQ
sources.locator: saved memories and separation from chat history
sources.support: Describes saved memories as details used in ChatGPT response context and stored separately from chat history.
sources.scopeLimit: ChatGPT-specific, account- and rollout-sensitive; it cannot define every product's memory.

claims.freshnessTrigger: Before prose review and release and whenever a named product's memory or retention controls are described.

claims.ruledClaim: Retrieval can fetch information after training and supply it for a response. It can support grounding, but the retrieved source can still be stale, incomplete, irrelevant, unauthorized or misunderstood; retrieval does not itself prove the answer.

sources.title: Machine Learning Glossary — grounding and retrieval-augmented generation
sources.support: Defines grounding through retrieved sources and RAG as providing a trained LLM access to retrieved knowledge.
sources.scopeLimit: The mechanism and intended benefit do not eliminate source-quality, permission, applicability or interpretation checks.

claims.freshnessTrigger: Any named retrieval product/source or claim that grounding guarantees correctness.

productionBoundaries.evergreenVsDated: The book owns stable mechanisms. Current chip markets, data-centre projects, energy quantities, provider features, prices and policy disputes belong in dated NewsStand applications linked back to the relevant mechanism.
productionBoundaries.analogyRule: Internet Explorer as the internet doorway and Miss Jeeves's working desk may be used only with explicit mappings and limits. They cannot replace the real system description.
productionBoundaries.providerBoundary: Provider documentation is a bounded example, never universal product behaviour.
productionBoundaries.releaseRule: Every exact prose claim must map to an exact supporting source excerpt; every provider-specific or numerical claim must be rechecked before self-review and release.
